title: Became or is? bli and vara with participles
goal: Tell apart something that happened (*blev stulen*) from the state it left behind (*är stulen*), and make participles agree like adjectives.
bekal: you can say what happened to something: *blev stulen*, *blev inbjuden*, *blev lagad*
you can describe a state with *är* + participle: *är stängd*, *är låst*, *är inställd*
you can make a participle agree: *stängd* / *stängt* / *stängda*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Cykeln är borta
dialogs.intro: A Sunday morning in the shared flat on Södermalm. Jonas, Elin's younger brother, comes back up the stairs much faster than he went down.

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Min cykel är borta. Den blev stulen i natt!
lines.id: My bike is gone. It got stolen last night!
lines.literal: my bike is gone. it became stolen in night!

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Nej, vad tråkigt! Var den inte låst?
lines.id: Oh no, that's awful! Wasn't it locked?
lines.literal: no, what boring! was it not locked?

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Jo, den var låst vid en lyktstolpe. Men någon klippte av låset.
lines.id: Yes, it was locked to a lamppost. But somebody cut the lock.
lines.literal: yes, it was locked at a lamppost. but someone cut off lock-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Har du anmält stölden till polisen?
lines.id: Have you reported the theft to the police?
lines.literal: have you reported theft-the to police-the?

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Ja, anmälan är redan gjord. Men de flesta stulna cyklar kommer aldrig tillbaka.
lines.id: Yes, the report's already been filed. But most stolen bikes never come back.
lines.literal: yes, report-the is already done. but the most stolen bikes come never back.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Stackars dig. Men du hade ju goda nyheter också, eller hur?
lines.id: You poor thing. But you had some good news too, didn't you?
lines.literal: poor you. but you had indeed good news too, or how?

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Ja! Vi har blivit inbjudna att spela på en klubb vid Hornstull i maj.
lines.id: Yes! We've been invited to play at a club near Hornstull in May.
lines.literal: yes! we have become invited to play at a club by Hornstull in May.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad roligt! Jag blir så glad för din skull.
lines.id: That's great! I'm so happy for you.
lines.literal: what fun! I become so glad for your sake.

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Tack. Allt är redan bestämt: datum, tid, allt.
lines.id: Thanks. Everything's already been decided: the date, the time, everything.
lines.literal: thanks. everything is already decided: date, time, everything.

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Men först behöver jag en ny cykel. Är cykelaffären på hörnet öppen idag?

lines.text: Nej, den är stängd på söndagar. Den öppnar igen imorgon klockan tio.

lines.literal: no, it is closed on Sundays. it opens again tomorrow clock-the ten.

lines.text: Typiskt. Då blir jag sen till repet ikväll.

lines.text: Ta min cykel! Den blev lagad i torsdags, så bromsarna fungerar.

lines.literal: take my bike! it became fixed in Thursday, so brakes-the work.

lines.text: Är du säker? Du är bäst, Dian.

lines.literal: are you sure? you are best, Dian.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Men lås den ordentligt. Och helst inte vid en lyktstolpe!

notes: **Den blev stulen** vs **den är stulen**. *Blev stulen* tells you what **happened** (the event, last night); *är stulen* describes the **situation now** (the bike is a stolen bike). A handy test: if English could say "got" — *it got stolen*, *we got invited*, *it got fixed* — Swedish wants **bli**. If English says "is" and means a state — *it's closed*, *it's locked* — Swedish wants **vara**.

**Stulna**, **inbjudna** — participles behave exactly like adjectives, so they take an ending for *ett*-words and for plurals. *Stulen* (one bike) becomes *stulna* (bikes), and *inbjuden* becomes *inbjudna* because *vi* is plural: *vi har blivit **inbjudna***. Stress the prefix: **IN-byüd-nah**.

**I natt** means "last night" when you talk about the past and "tonight" when you talk about the future: *den blev stulen i natt* (last night), *jag sover hos Oskar i natt* (tonight). The same family gives you **i morse** (**i MOSH-eh**, "this morning", only about the past) and **i torsdags** ("last Thursday") from Unit 1.

**Anmälan är gjord** — "the report has been filed", literally "is done". *Gjord / gjort / gjorda* is the irregular participle of *göra*, and **Det är gjort** ("It's done") is a phrase you will hear daily. *En anmälan* is one of those *-an* nouns that look the same with and without the article: *en anmälan*, *anmälan* (the report).

**Jag blir så glad för din skull** — "I'm so happy for you". Swedes use **bli** for feelings that **start** because of something: *jag blir glad*, *han blev arg*, *hon blev besviken*. English often says "is" or "gets" here; Swedish nearly always says *bli*. *För din skull* means "for your sake": *för min skull*, *för hans skull*.

**Stackars dig** ("you poor thing") — *stackars* (**STAHK-kahsh**) never changes its form: *stackars Jonas*, *stackars cykeln*, *stackars oss*. And **repet** is the band's *rep*, short for *repetition*, "rehearsal" — a false friend: *en repetition* is a rehearsal, not a repetition in the English sense.

grammars.title: bli or vara?
body: Read each row left to right: first the event, then the state it leaves behind. The participle is the same; only the verb in front of it changes.
after: *Bli* works in every tense: *blir* (gets, will get), *blev* (got), *har blivit* (has got). *Vi **har blivit** inbjudna* = we've been invited, and the invitation is still news.

*Bli* + participle is Swedish's **second passive**. In Unit 5 you met the s-passive: *Cykeln stals i natt*. Both are correct; *blev stulen* sounds more like everyday speech and puts the focus on what happened to the bike. Signs, news and instructions prefer the s-passive.
*Bli* + adjective means "become": *bli sjuk* (fall ill), *bli trött*, *bli kär* (fall in love). That is the same verb doing the same job — showing a change.

grammars.title: Participles agree like adjectives
body: A past participle has three forms, exactly like *stor / stort / stora*: one for *en*-words, one for *ett*-words, and one for plurals and definite forms. Which ending you need depends on the verb group.
after: Agreement follows the noun: *Dörren är stäng**d**. Fönstret är stäng**t**. Fönstren är stäng**da**.* And in front of a noun, the definite form: *den stäng**da** dörren*, *de stul**na** cyklarna*.

Watch the strong verbs: the **supine** ends in *-it*, the **participle** in *-et*. *Jag har skriv**it** brevet* (I have written the letter) — but *Brevet är skriv**et*** (the letter is written). Learners mix these up for years; now you know the trap.
With a particle verb, the particle jumps to the front and joins the participle: *bjuda in* → *inbjuden*, *ställa in* → *inställd*. You will meet many more in Svenska 103.

blocks.text: Walk down any street in Stockholm and you will read participles all day long — on shop doors, station screens and parking signs. Notice that most signs use the **ett**-form: *Stängt*, *Öppet*, *Inställt*. That is because the hidden subject is *det* ("it", the situation): *Det är stängt*.
Look at the last two rows: *rökning* and *parkering* are *en*-words, so the participle takes the *en*-form: *förbjuden*.

blocks.title: Feelings that start: bli + adjective
items: *bli glad* (be pleased) · *bli ledsen* (get upset) · *bli arg* (get angry)
*bli rädd* (get scared) · *bli förvånad* (be surprised) · *bli besviken* (be disappointed)
*bli trött* (get tired) · *bli sjuk* (fall ill) · *bli kär* (fall in love)
Make them agree, too: *Vi blev **glada***. *Barnen blev **rädda***.

sections.title: When things go wrong: theft, repairs, cancellations

blocks.text: Bike theft is so common in Swedish cities that most people simply expect it sooner or later. If it happens, you file an *anmälan* with the police (online, it takes five minutes) and send the number to your home insurance, *hemförsäkringen*, which usually pays part of the value.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 5
items: Turn each s-passive into a *bli*-passive: *Cykeln stals.* → *Cykeln blev stulen.* *Konserten ställdes in.* → *Konserten blev inställd.* *Vi bjöds in.* → *Vi blev inbjudna.*
Then describe the state with *är*: *Cykeln är stulen. Konserten är inställd. Vi är inbjudna.*
Notice which one you would write on a sign and which one you would say to a friend.
